utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Lausic, I would like to remind you - it may sound familiar in your ears now - I'd like it remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Misetic will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I'd like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is 1D66-0260, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think you've seen this document in quite a long time so I will give you an opportunity to read through it, and then I'd just like it ask you a few questions about it. It's from the 3rd of April, 1995, and it's correspondence between you and the commander of the southern front of the Juzno Bojiste. Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try. The distance doesn't agree with me, but, still ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page then. Okay. If we could now have the English back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Lausic, what appears to be -- have happened here is that the -- in April of 1995, the commander of the southern front claimed authority under Article 9 to deploy military police units to guard a military facility, and you corresponded with him and instructed him that in fact he did not have that authority. Can you explain to us what exactly your role is there, in ensuring the property use of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm not sure your interpretation of my words to the commander of Southern Front is correct. You said that I told him that he could not use the military police under Article 9, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, for this particular facility.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is a facility which should have been secured in accordance with the rules governing features that are to be secured by guards, rather than deploying the military police, which is not cost-effective in this case. They are too expensive for this sort of job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But why is it you that gets to oversee how a military commander is deploying the military police? What gave you the authority to make that review?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While touring the 6th company of the 72nd battalion in Dubrovnik, I came to the conclusion that despite the great number of tasks they were charged with and the few numbers of men that the company had, the commander of the Southern Front used the few human resources he had in an inappropriate manner. In this letter, I cautioned him that he was invoking Article 9 on the daily operational command employed by the military police for such duties as are not foreseen under the rules governing the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it safe to say, then, under Article 8, you have the ability to overrule the deployment of the military police that a commander may invoke under Article 9 of the rules?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police administration and the vertical system of subordination of MP units, vis-a-vis the MP administration, as I've already noted in my statements and testimony, primarily had the task of preventing the misuse or abuse of the military police. Fortunately, in this particular instance it only came down to an inadequate or inappropriate use of the military police and non-cost-effective. Whereas, in the previous years there were cases of a more drastic nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 1D66-0260 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in your list, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1288.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I'd like to go back to the rules for a few minutes. And if you could take look at Articles 10 and 11 of Exhibit P880, please. Now, Article 10, subpart 9 -- wait for it in the English. Subpart 9 says: "Participation in carrying out combat tasks on the front line, pursuant to orders by the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia," that that is one of the jobs and tasks of the military police. Do you agree that a military commander under Article 9 cannot deploy the military police in combat tasks unless he has -- unless there is an order to that effect allowing him to do so by the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, pursuant to the orders of the minister of defence, the minister himself, not the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. You agree; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the rules say. It's not for me to agree or disagree with. It was signed by the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go to Article 11, it says: "The primary purpose of the anti-terrorist units of the military police is to carry out tasks, as contained in Article 9, items 8 and 9 of the Rules, and to carry out other tasks from the scope of activities of the military police, as required." Now, my first question is, do you agree that Article 11 here has a typo and that it should say "to carry out the tasks theas contained in Article 10, items 8 and 9."

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. I don't know what sort of copy we have enclosed here. It's the original. Well, I think that when the rules were published in a booklet, the typo was corrected. But absolutely, yes, that's true. Article 10, that's what the Article 11 should read, and not Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that deployment of the anti-terrorist units for combat task would have required the -- an order from the minister of defence under Article 10, subpart 9?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Looking at Article 10, subpart 2, as one of the jobs and tasks of the military police, it talks about prevention and uncovering of crimes, identification and arrest of perpetrators of crimes that fall within the jurisdiction of military judiciary bodies, et cetera, et cetera. Now, I'd like to draw your attention to Rule 54 of the rules, which is page 23 in the B/C/S, and 23 in the English as well. Now, Article 54 says: "If there is any suspicion that a crime was committed that falls within the jurisdiction of a military court, authorised military police officials must take the necessary steps to find the perpetrators of the crime, to prevent the perpetrator or co-perpetrator from hiding or absconding, and to locate and preserve traces of the crime and objects that can serve as evidence, and gather any information that might be useful for a successful criminal investigation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page. Go to Article 55. It says: "The duties from Article 54 of these rules shall be performed by the authorised official of the military police unit with territorial jurisdiction, ex officio, by request of the state prosecutor in charge or by request of a court."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, finally, if we can go to page 27, to Article 66 through 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "On the basis of the information gathered, when there are grounds for suspicion that a crime was committed, an authorised official of the military police shall draft a criminal report providing a description of the crime and listing the evidence obtained during the process of information gathering." Now, under Article 55, as I understand it, a member of the crime police of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, for example, did not need an order from you, in order to conduct an investigation. Correct? By nature of his job, once he receives information that there is a suspicion, he is duty-bound to investigation that allegation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you specifically refer to the following levels, and I will start from the lowest level, the investigator officer of the criminal investigation section of the 72nd Battalion. Are you referring to the chief of the section of the criminal investigation military police of the 72nd Battalion, or are you referring to the commander of the 72nd Battalion which had, as its part, the section and the officers I referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, under Article 55 it says that the duties under Article 54 shall be performed by the authorised official of the military police unit with territorial jurisdiction ex officio. Are any of the military police members that you have just identified persons who would not be considered authorised officials of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who held the status of an authorised official are mentioned in the system of the 72nd Military Police Battalion as such, as was indeed the case with all the other ones of all the other units. Certain members of the military police units did not have the status of authorised officials. Since what is referred to here is an authorised official, by that token, it refers to the authorised officials of the military police because only they, under these rules, had the right to exercise these particular military police powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking now of the authorised military police officials. Under Article 55, they were to act pursuant to a request of a state prosecutor in charge or by request of a court, or ex officio. And what I'm asking you is, if that authorised military police official received information, as indicated in Article 66 or under Article 54, that there was a suspicion that a crime was committed, he was obligated to take the necessary steps to find the perpetrator of the crime. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That authorised military police official did not need a separate order from you, for example, to tell him to go and take the necessary steps to find the perpetrator. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is understood that way, yes. Of course, not -- at least not at my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Similarly -- well, even at your level if you had information that a crime had been committed which falls within the jurisdiction of the military court, you could pass that information on to the relevant authorised military police official in the area, and they were duty-bound to take the necessary steps to find the perpetrator. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you clarify the question. I'm not quite clear. Based on your question, if I had information about a criminal offence having been committed, I would convey that information to the police unit which has territorial jurisdiction for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Either to them or to your chief of the crime military police.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first level of my contact would be the chief of the crime investigation department at the police -- at the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And once you passed the information to them, they were duty-bound by the rules and the law to take the necessary steps to find the perpetrator. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To take certain operational steps and actions to shed light on the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Similarly, a military commander in the field, if he learns of a crime, or has information that a crime was committed, a suspicion, he has to alert the authorised military police official to take the -- so that they can take the necessary steps to find the perpetrator. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He is duty-bound like any citizen of the Republic of Croatia to report a suspected crime under the Criminal Code of the Republic of Croatia. Any citizen has the duty to do that. In this case, this is a commander. But it's the duty and obligation of every citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is no need for a commander to issue an order to the authorised military police official to conduct an investigation, because the authorised military police official is already under a legal obligation to take the necessary steps to find the perpetrator of the crime. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes well, it also depends on the form in which this information is conveyed because in the army information, especially if conveyed by their commander, is in the form of an order. He can't write a request or a letter. He issues an order. In the preamble of the order, he sets out the circumstances of the incident, according to his information, issues an order, and, based on his knowledge, action is taken to elucidate the crime. It would be unusual for a commander to write a letter or a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lausic, if it was in the form of an order or a letter or a request, as a legal matter, it makes no refreshes to the authorise the military official in what form he receives the information because is he an under a legal duty to take all necessary steps to find the perpetrator of the crime, whether he received an order to do that, whether he received a letter, whether he received it in any other form. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I'd like to take you to Exhibit P972, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And we will use the -- the Prosecution has uploaded three separate English translations, Mr. President, four separate English translations. The first I'd like to use is the first English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lausic, this is the handbook on the work and procedures of the Republic of Croatia armed forces military crime police. And it's in Zagreb from 1996. But I'm sure you're familiar with this handbook. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You seem -- it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... actually signed by the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been accompanied by a letter of mine, about if it's signed by the minister of defence, then there's no doubt. But I always submitted to him for signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 9 in the English, page ... there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the bottom, in number 10 it says: "While performing their duties and tasks, the military crime police shall cooperate with the military prosecutor's office, military court, county courts, the security and information service of the Republic of Croatia Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, and other elements within the security system of the Republic of Croatia. "The military crime police shall inform these bodies of all issues that are of interest to them or are of importance for public order and security, and they shall do this at their own initiative or at the request of the bodies referred to in paragraph 1 of this item."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could now go to the fourth English translation, paragraph 112. It's page 36 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "It is the duty of the military crime police to file criminal reports submitted for crimes that are prosecuted ex officio. The criminal report shall immediately be forwarded to the competent military prosecutor. "Any information in written or oral form pointing to a crime or possible crime to the perpetrator of a crime and to evidence and items relating to the crime and perpetrator shall be considered to be a criminal report." Now, paragraph 112, was this the policy and procedure that was in effect in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not give you a precise answer. This was passed in 1996, when the work of the military crime police, which was a very young specialty, was being promoted and improved, also based on the experience gained in 1995 during the liberation of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, this document is a format taken over from the civilian crime police, the same modality of work. But to your question, whether this format was fully applied in 1995, I could not answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lausic, let me show you a different exhibit. This is P1116.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is page 51 in the English and page 43 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, this is the Law on Defence from 1993 which was in effect in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I'm interested in Article 145.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the first two paragraphs there: "For the safety of citizens and property and to protect the interest of defence, during military exercises, the Defence Minister or the commander authorised by him may restrict freedom of movement in the area in which the exercise is being conducted and in cooperation with the authorised state administrative body, he may define measures and procedures to secure that area. "In wartime, the military commander and officer in the position of regiment commander or a commander at the same or a higher level may temporarily restrict freedom of movement in the area, zone, and territory where preparations for combat operations are being made." Now, under this provision and under your understanding pursuant to your powers under Article 8 and a commanders powers under Article 9, a military commander could use the military police to set up a check-point to block and restrict freedom of movement only in an area where combat operations are being prepared. Is that correct? I'm talking about the military commander and not the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Article does not specify with what forces or what units this is restriction of movement would be enforced in a certain area. It only says that he has the right to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Precisely because these questions are not answered in the Article is why I'm asking you based on your experience in the military police, whether a commander, pursuant to Article 145, could deploy the military police to restrict freedom of movement in an area where preparations for combat operations are being made.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with Article 9, he could issue such orders to the battalion commander, and that is the prerogative of commanders of Military Districts including the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's where I'm going next, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit P1143, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by then Brigadier Ademi on the 18th of August to Major Budimir, and he orders him, in point 1, to set up a check-point at the Knin Gracac Otric cross-roads. And in point three he says: "Only motor vehicles with a regular PRL are to be allowed through the check-point into the zone of operative group west while the entry of civilian motor vehicles into the zone" --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Work paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... while the entry of civilian motor vehicles into the zone is strictly forbidden." Now, do you agree with me that under Article 145, Brigadier Ademi could order such a check-point but could not limit the access of civilians to the area unless this zone was in fact an area where combat operations were being prepared?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit, I don't understand your question again. This is a classical order where the right to command the military police is exercised under Article 9, and the micro location is identified for the check-point and tasks for that check-point are identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no note --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you don't understand my question, let me rephrase it. Because then if you give an answer to a question you don't understand, we drift off. My question is, that, yes, this order can be issued to the military police. But my question to you is that, under the Law on Defence, a commander can only issue such an order to restrict movement within an area that is in fact a zone where preparations for combat operations are being made.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this order was written on the 18th of August. And on the 7th of August, the civilian authorities power was already pro claimed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I assumed, maybe incorrectly, that you're familiar with the fact that in this time-period the HV was conducting operations in Bosnia. And I might refresh your recollection with the incident of around 15 HV soldiers being killed in Derala around this time-period. Does that refresh your recollection? Do you remember an incident after Operation Storm where 15 HV soldiers were killed in a Bosnian Serb action in the area known as Derala, where 15 men from the Katala area were killed? You don't remember this?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. Lausic. Let's talk a little bit about the anti-terrorist platoon. And I think we already looked at Article 11 which talked about -- Article 11 of the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Registrar, I'd like it pull up 65 ter 359, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order that you issued to all military police units concerning the deployment of the military police anti-terrorist units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Military police anti-terrorist units shall not be used in performing regular military police tasks except in special circumstances and upon approval by the chief of the military police administration." Now, my first question is: This order was no withdrawn by the time of Operation Storm, was it? It was still in effect.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell you precisely. I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I generally remember there order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you don't need -- I know you probably do know, but I'm trying to finish soon. So I don't need the background; I just wanted to know if this order, to your knowledge, was still in effect in August, and your answer is ... I'm not sure I understood what your answer was. Was it in effect in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not answer your question because it's an order from March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The phraseology says: "Shall not be used in performing regular military policing tasks, and except in special circumstances and upon approval by the chief of the military police administration?" Am I correct in my interpretation that pursuant to that provision, a military commander could not use the anti-terrorist platoons under Article 9 without your permission?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could ask permission from the battalion commander in his Military District to use an anti-terrorist platoon or company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat. I'm not sure we got the full answer. You said he could go to the battalion commander, and then the battalion commander would do what, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would ask for approval that this anti-terrorist unit be used for duties specified in the order of the commander of the Military District, which, if I'm not mistaken, was done in the case of the 72nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who specifically would he ask for approval?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who? You mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the battalion would seek approval from whom for the use of the anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at paragraph 2.4 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually the introduction at paragraph 2 says: "Military police anti-units shall be primarily involved in a training process as well as for the following tasks." And then 2.4 says: "For execution of combat activities of the HV in searching and mopping up the terrain behind the HV units, further to the orders issued by the military police administration." 2.5 says: "For offensive combat activities within the military police units' area of responsibility or as a joint military police formation, further to order issued by the Republic of Croatia Defence Minister." Pursuant to this order, the anti-terrorist units could only be engaged in searching and mopping up the terrain pursuant to orders issued by the military police administration. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have interpretation -- or, rather, translations into Croatian only up to point 2.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we could turn the page, Mr. Registrar, in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document 65 ter 359 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1289.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1289 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, let me show you two documents in a row, and then I'll ask for your comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first is 65 ter 3148, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is a request of the 4th of January, 1995, by General Gotovina to you. And I'd ask you to read it, and when you've finished reading it, let me know and I will show you the second document.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, please. I can't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could put the English version on the screen, Mr. Registrar, for the benefit of the Chamber. And now, Mr. Registrar, if we could have 1D66-0256, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what I'm showing you now, Mr. Lausic, is your response to General Gotovina's request from the 5th of January, 1995. And I'd ask you to read this, and let me know when you've finished reading it.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My question to you is, if you can explain to the Court what's happening there. What is General Gotovina asking for you, and why did you deny the request?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a precise answer. This is a joint company active in Bosnia-Herzegovina. General Gotovina seeks approval for the use of that particular MP company. In my response, I refer him to the chief of the MP administration of the Ministry of Defence of the -- Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna which has that particular joint company at its disposal. In the last paragraph I emphasise the fact that should there be any need for the deployment of military police forces, and I was referring to additional forces, that we would jointly agree upon this with the MP administration of the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Why can't General Gotovina just issue his own order and use the joint military police company pursuant to his own order and without your consent?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see here, it has nothing to do with my consent. This joint company was under the jurisdiction of the chief of the MP administration of the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna which existed as such at the time. Its purpose was to carry out special tasks; namely, securing special convoys in -- as part of Operation Pauk which was under way at the time. This was a special purpose company for special tasks. I did not reject his request. I merely referred him to the MP administration of Herceg-Bosna which had that particular company under its competence. And that should he have any need for additional forces, we would be dealing with that and resolving that problem. The area involved is that of a neighbouring republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 65 ter 3148 and 1D66-0256 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 03148 becomes Exhibit D1290. And document 1D66-0256 becomes Exhibit D1291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1290 and D1291 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, let me turn you back to your diary which is Exhibit P2166 at page 2, please. This is the entry for the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the bottom. If we could turn the page, please, in English. There we go. At the bottom, in the Croatian, and page 1 of the B/C/S. The date is the 29th of April at the bottom, I believe. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The English still seems to be for April 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 2 in the English, please. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now it says the request by Major-General Ante Gotovina has been approved. And then there's all sorts of entries. Number 6 says: "Place the anti-terrorist military police of the 72nd Military Police Battalion under the Split Military District Command." Is this an example, Mr. Lausic, of General Gotovina having to seek permission from you, in order to be able to use the anti-terrorist unit of the 72nd Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As these amount to short notes taken at the meeting held on the 29th of April, 1995, in the afternoon hours in the offices of the chief of the Main Staff, in the run-up to Operation Flash, I don't know, and I can't give you a precise answer in relation to chapter 2. In other words, who it was who said what was reflected in these notes about the request from General Gotovina and about requests being granted. I don't know if it was the chief of the Main Staff. At any rate I do believe that the issues were resolved in the way prescribed by the rules on the use of the military police forces and anti-terrorist forces. If it was the minister of defence who was the one giving his consent for their deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, it can't be the chief of the Main Staff to approve that request because under the rules that can only be done by the minister of defence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if General Gotovina's request was conveyed to the minister of defence from my level or from the chief of the Main Staff's level. I'm merely setting out the fact that the request for the use of this particular anti-terrorist platoon was granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now go to page 38 of this document in the English and page 33 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is this your entry, Mr. Lausic, I believe, for the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, it might be the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's the 8th of August, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in the Croatian, please. We were on the right page in the English there, so ... there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you have a handwritten -- or a note in your notebook, and it says: "Draft command on placing in reserve the anti-terrorist platoon of the 71st military police and the anti-terrorist platoon of the 72nd Military Police. Have them take a three- to five-day leave followed by possible deployment." Can you tell us, was that an order that you received from the minister of defence to withdraw the anti-terrorist units?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go back to the date when military police units were taken out of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was going to show that you document next, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D837. If we could have that on the, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was the 9th, which is the next day, which is when your order is then issued. So if this is on the 8th, you are making a note that you have draft an order?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So would that entry mean that you were told by the minister of defence to withdraw the anti-terrorist platoons?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To withdraw all military police units from combat. And it was primarily the anti-terrorist platoons that were in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now we have your order which was then written the next day and issued on the screen. It goes to all the military police units. The subject is "disengagement of the military police units from combat activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Point 1 is: "All military police units engaged in combat activities are to be disengaged from the areas of combat activities at 0700 hours on the 10th of August." Now, I'm correct, am I not, that that doesn't just refer to the anti-terrorist platoons; that refers to Article 10 of the rules which requires the consent of the minister of defence for any military police unit to be engaged in combat activity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, point 2, and this, I believe, is a mistranslation in the English, refers to the "anti-tank platoons," and I think it should be anti-terrorist platoons, "and other members of the military police participating in combat activities are to be given respite during 10th and 11th August. And as of 12 August, at 0700, in the area of responsibility of the military police, the same are to be engaged in search (mopping up) of the liberated territory ..." So you then, in fact, did issue the order to remove the anti-terrorist platoons and put them on respite. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what follows from the order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could go to Exhibit P1208, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order that Mr. Tieger showed you in direct examination from the 10th. And it's not issued to the military police. You can see in the upper right-hand corner, Brigadier Glasnovic is not a member of the military police. You're aware of that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that it was not sent to military police units or the MP administration. I don't know what Brigadier Glasnovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But General Gotovina now refers to the order that was issued by you, which we just had on the screen, and it says: "In order to use the military police and the anti-terrorist units in the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia in the way that is appropriate to the purpose I hereby order ..." Now, what General Gotovina is doing there is telling his commander in the field that he has received an order which basically withdrew the consent of the minister of defence to use military police for combat purposes and to use the anti-terrorist unit for combat purposes and, therefore, the forces of the Split Military District had to ensure that those forces were not engaged in any combat activity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Split Military District, as did all the other Military District Commanders, received this particular order of mine for their information. I did not order anything to them but to MP units. That's what it says here, to receive for their information. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... isn't this another example when we talk about coordination between the military police administration and the military line, I absolutely agree with that you could you not issue an order to General Gotovina. But, nevertheless, because he could only use the military police for combat purposes with the consent of the minister of defence, if the minister of defence withdrew his consent, he had no alternative but to remove those units from combat activity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you what sort of alternatives he had. There were other alternatives, but he did what he was duty-bound to do as a commander. There were situations when it was not done this way, and I'm not referring to General Gotovina; I'm referring to some other individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go now to 65 ter 568, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is now on the 11th of August and is a report from you to the minister of defence as well as to -- to General Cervenko and others identified in the header. And in the first paragraph, you advise that: "The members of the anti-terrorist formations of the military police and the parts of the general military police who participated in combat activities in the Operation Oluja during 10 August 1995 have been withdrawn and directed for a 24-hour leave to subsequently be engaged on mopping up." Mr. Lausic, do you recall this document and, in fact, were you here reporting to the minister of defence and the Chief of Staff that the order to withdraw military police from combat had in fact been implemented?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need to comment upon that at all. You can read the first paragraph to see what I'm reporting to them. And since it is an original document, there is no need for me to comment on whether it is it authenticate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 65 ter 568 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a bar table document, Your Honour, so I understand there is no objection in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, let me just ask you about OA Varivode one more time. Do you have any knowledge or information that a commander of the 4th Company Sibenik, Commander Mrkota attempted to cover up or obstruct the investigation against a certain individual named Goran Vunic. Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At any time were you made aware of any suspicion that someone in the military police engaged in OA Varivode was engaging in any activity that might be construed as obstructing the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I would like to show you a video now which is a press conference held by Mr. Jarnjak and Mr. Benko in late October after OA Varivode had been under way for sometime. I'd just ask to you listen to it and see if you agree that this was the information about the statistics of crime that was in the possession of the Croatian security apparatus as of 18 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is 1D66-0254, for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Ivan Jarnjak: Crimes which were committed in those areas were documented and are undergoing crime processing or have been processed up to now. Mr. Benko will comment on this later, and this was conducted in cooperation with the military police in the field. The most common form of documented crimes were arson and aggravated theft, and then there were the gravest crimes which are murders. What created the greatest concern amongst the public was the news of the murders in the villages of Varivode and Gosici, which have been solved. The perpetrators have been apprehended, and Mr. Benko will comment on this issue later today. "Marijan Benko: In two cases in two cases of robbery where we -- or, rather, 41 murders were reported, 25 were solved. The murders in the villages of Varivode and Gosici were of particular interest where seven civilians were killed in Gosici and 9 in Varivode. After conducting crime processing in cooperation with the military police, we identified the perpetrators of these crimes, apprehended them, and transferred them to the investigating centre of the county court of Zadar. In the newly liberated areas, 844 cases of aggravated theft have been processed, 619 of which have been solved, and 751 persons have had reports filed against them. "Ivan Jarnjak: We have taken all the steps to protect these people, both the people and their property. And there is no reason to remove them from their homes and transfer them to some kind of collection centres or such-like. We shall create and we have already created the preconditions for them to peacefully and safely live in their homes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, do you recall that press conference?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't have it present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a reference there that by the 18th of October in cooperation with the military police persons had been apprehended in connection with the murders at Varivode and Gosici. Can you confirm that that was the case, that that was done in cooperation with the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, on Thursday or Friday we saw a report sent to me from the commander of Action Varivode. I don't know the date was, but it was your document. Colonel Kozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And was the -- were the statistics that were referred to there, was that consistent with your understanding of the statistics of solved and unsolved crime in the liberated territories as of the 18th of October?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will tender the video, 1D66-025.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1292.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1292 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one more document to show. Unfortunately, we acquired it over the weekend. So we do now have it in e-court. Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D66-0309, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is from the 15th of August, 1995. It is the conclusions reached at the regular weekly meeting of the military police administration, department chiefs, and heads of sections from the 14th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could flip to the second-to-last page in English, please. Numbered page 7 in the Croatian, please, which I think is third from the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is on the 14th of August, and Mr. Juric had obviously returned back from the field on the 14th because the notes indicate that he was present at the weekly meeting in Zagreb. If you'd read through what Mr. Juric said, you will see that he doesn't mention any particular problems with soldiers committing crime in the area. He does say -- the notes say he also pointed out the problem of cooperation with members of the RH MUP to which General Lausic responded that all problems and disagreements with the members of the MUP, MORH, Ministry Of Defence officials, and others are to be presented in a summary report and the deadline for the deliver of the same for all responsible officers in the MP administration is 20 August 1995. "General Lausic complemented in general the work of the forward command posts and their formation showed to be justified." Do you remember this meeting on the 14th? And do you remember Mr. Juric being present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I had the meeting of my collegium every Monday, and minutes were taken at each and every one of them, and I can't remember the details of one such minute. But if this is what you found in the archives of the military police administration, which I believe you did, complete with the signatures on the last page, then I have no reason to doubt the authenticity of the statements contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 1D66-0309.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1293, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Lausic, I just wanted to ask you about your diary that you kept. Can you tell us generally why that wasn't something that you turned over to the state archive?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you the same answer I gave to the ICTY investigators in May 2004. This is not a diary of mine. It is a work notebook where I jotted down my daily private and official contacts, the private chores I had to attend to, as well as my notes which I transcribed onto official documents which had to do with my role in the work -- in the run-up to Operation Flash and Storm as well as in relation to the 1993 Medak-pocket operation. For that reason it is my own document and not a document for the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answering all my questions. You have been very patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. One question about translation of something you just read to the witness. It reads: "General Lausic complemented in general the work of" -- should that be "complimented" instead of "complemented"? I can't see the original, but I have some difficulties in understanding c-o-m-p-l-e, or should it be "I"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My second grade spelling teacher is not going to be angry with me, Judge, but I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I am not a native-speaking person, but I have difficulties in understanding complemented here instead of complimented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Without commenting on the evidence, I think in that context it would be with an "I," meaning praised or -- rather than supplemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll correct that, Mr. President, and upload a different version into e-court then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If there's no objection, I think there's one of the earlier documents I showed which said -- translated AT unit as anti-tank unit, and I think it should be anti-terrorist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, if it would have been AT, because it was in an abbreviation, where elsewhere in that document we find written in its entirety the anti-terrorist unit. So where AT is written, I would completely -- I take it there is no objection against this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll wait for that. Mr. Lausic, we'll have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you are next in line. Mr. Lausic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First matter I want to look at with you, Mr. Lausic, concerns the issue of regular tasks, special tasks, the various phrases that have been used in orders. And if we can start by looking at a document, 2D08-0007. This is a document dated the 1st of May, 1995. It's issued by you to the military police battalions and delivered elsewhere, and you can see that the subject is the involvement of the military police in the zones of responsibility. First of all, do you recollect issuing this order?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's connected to the commencement of the Flash operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2 of the English and look at paragraph 5, or point 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see there - next page in the Croatian language - I'll read out 5. It says: "Carry out regular military police tasks in accordance with Article 9 of the mentioned order along with adjusting rotational system of work to the tasks of the MP units." Would I be right in saying that that is a classic expression of the command under Article 9 being expressed?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 9 of the rules on the system and method of work of the military police, this was implied. You did not specify Article 9 of what regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see the use of the word "regular," which appears in Article 9, and there you use the precise legal provision from the rules of the military police, as I said, in a classic textbook form of expression. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've no need to look further at that document. And may that documenting be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. Just wanted to note that at the outset, Mr. Kay mentioned that it was issued to the battalions. I think it indicates battalions and companies. I didn't want to interrupt the flow of his questioning for that minor correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it there is it no need to further comment on that. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1294.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1294 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we return to a document that we looked at last week, Exhibit D267, and this is the order you issued on the 2nd of August, Mr. Lausic, again, to the battalions of the military police. It's the preparation order ending in reference 466. We're just waiting for the English to turn up. And there's the document we're very familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 2 and look at paragraph 3 on page 2, and look at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's the second part of paragraph 3 where it says: "Within the daily operational chain of command, commanders of military police battalions shall be subordinated to commanders of the Military Districts." And if we look at 4, the second sentence: "Within the daily operational chain of command, company commanders shall be subordinated to commanders of the operation groups of the Croatian army." Now, the phrase "daily operational chain of command" is not within Article 8, nor within Article 9. It is another expression entirely, and it is to do with the command system. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "daily" -- regular. Sorry, regular tasks, implies the execution of all tasks from the purview of the military police; whereas, the word "daily operational command" implies that the commander of the Military District and all these levels mentioned in these Articles may, on a daily basis, issue orders to execute tasks from the purview of the military police. Daily operational, we know what the word "operational," "operation" means. That means performing a task, a mission, a duty. There is no contradiction between these two terms. Because the word "regular" is understood to mean the purview of the military police and "daily operational" refers to the daily issuing of assignments and tasks to perform operational duties. There is no contradiction. It's a terminological difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just if we could look at that a little bit closer because we come to this to analyse these documents. The daily operational chain of command does not necessarily mean, then, regular.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers primarily to regular tasks, but they may be also extraordinary tasks, such as providing extraordinary security that had not been planned for a given time or participation in the execution of an action that had not been planned. But what is important is that it falls within the purview of the military police. That is the standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Although it's right that, under Article 9, the only command and control is in relation to regular tasks, regular military police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the witness is waiting for a specific question, Your Honour. I know Mr. Kay intended it that way, but I think from the witness's expression it wasn't understood to call for a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the transcript the question mark is also missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I apologise. And took it the question mark would be understood. There was a question mark at the end. And that is right, isn't it? I will add.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can look now at point 12 of the same order. So next page in the Croatian and page 4 of the English. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we have actually part of 10 we can look at. The second-to-last sentence of 10, where it says: "Within the operative chain of command, Colonel Damir Kozic shall be subordinated to the commander of the Main Staff in the forward command post in Ogulin." And it goes on further. And then in 12, we can see commanding and reporting system within the daily operational chain of command, commanders of military police battalions, other commanders "shall be subordinated to," and if we turn over the page in English, just to complete the document, page 5, and the last section of paragraph 12 in this document, Mr. Lausic, gives the reporting system under this order. Again, the phrase there "daily operational chain of command," did you mean by that all tasks of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Everything that belongs within the competences of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that would be regular and special tasks or extraordinary tasks as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. If extraordinary tasks fell within the purview of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could look at the next document now, still on this subject, which is Exhibit D1282.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's another document dated the 2nd of August, 1995, issued by you on that day. It's the one that ends in 470, and it concerns the military police treatment of foreigners and media representatives. We've looked at it previously, but I want to just see about this matter in the subject, where it says: "Military police members, while performing everyday military police tasks concerning security, patrol, check-points, who are in contact with foreigners." There we see another phrase "everyday," and what I'd like you to explain is what you mean by that in the context of the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Execution of military police tasks that are performed continuously every day, or based on specific orders given as part of exercising rights envisaged by the Articles on daily operational command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would this include regular as well as special tasks?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. But those that are performed every day, continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If a special task is done a day -- on an everyday basis, that would be included. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we now go to -- I can move on now to the 5th of August. Exhibit P881, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the 5th of August. It's the 485 document, Mr. Lausic. Again, a document we're familiar with. It is the -- upon successful completion of the Operation Oluja, and it's to the companies and battalions of the military police to their commanders, and it concerns the establishment of the military police units. We see at 1.5, something we're familiar with. The military police company in Knin being established as well as a company in Benkovac and in Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to page 2 of the English and look at paragraph 7 of the document, it states: "For the execution of daily operations, the commanders of the newly established military police units shall be subordinated to the most senior ... commander in their respective zone of responsibility." For completeness, this is the order we know that was issued by you. And shall we just look at paragraph 7 then. First of all, looking at the subordination, the phrase is used there of "to the most senior Croatian army commander in their respective zone of responsibility." But we know from Article 9 that, actually, it says "to the highest Croatian army commander by function" in the military police units area of operation. Are you able to explain why the full text of Article 9 was not used within this paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer this question, but the issue is purely terminological.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When we see at the beginning of paragraph 7 "execution of daily operations, the commanders of the newly established military police units," what do we mean by "daily operations" there? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daily execution of tasks that fall within the purview of the military police in a certain area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm told by someone who knows the language better than me that the original would read according to the text that we've previously been looking at, Your Honour, using that phrase "daily operational command" rather than "daily operations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just as handicapped as you are in this respect, and I take it my fellow Judges as well. So if there's any -- any need to have it either -- if the translation is wrong then, of course, we should seek that. If the original language is not very precise then, of course, it's a matter of interpretation. And if the parties could agree on it, fine. If not, then the Chamber will have to -- if need be, have to determine the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we can just clear that up now, as I know Mr. Tieger has an expert to his right, in the sense of a language speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I'm not -- normally -- well, for certain matters I'll resolve it that way. If the question is whether or not the language in Croatian in the -- in that specific item is the same as a previous document where the translation was "daily operational command," I guess we're in a position to gauge that. I think, as I understand it, the language in the Croatian is the same. But I -- now the question is, which of the two interpretations in English is the more proper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I suggest the following: There are too much ifs and ands to resolve the matter immediately. The next break would perhaps be a better opportunity, or this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do regret that, Your Honour, but we have to -- I want to make a clear question to the witness. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't want -- if you read it in -- if it is read to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll get the witness to read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The easier way because we're not being able to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you read out paragraph 7, please, Mr. Lausic, so that we can hear it over our headphones.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 7: "The commanders of the newly established military police units shall, in the daily operational command, be subordinated to the most senior commander of the Croatian army in their area of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We got there. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, so that would be regular as well as special tasks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But I have to stress once more that if the extraordinary tasks, and I don't want to refer to them as special tasks, if they fall within the purview of the military police, the terms "special" and "extraordinary" differ in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. The problem by leaving out "most senior commander by function," you said that was just terminological. But what is the commander of the battalion supposed to understand in relation to the command and control of him?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander can never have such a dilemma because his commander is the commander of the Military District within whose area of responsibility he is present by virtue of the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it comes down to who he reports to. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a commander of the military police battalion, yes, that goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us now look at another document, 65 ter 5814.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document not from you, but it's from a Commander Jenjic of the 72nd Military Police Battalion of the 5th Company, and he sends a document, a report to Major Juric on the 8th of August. First of all, is this a document that you have ever seen before?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This type of document which would be a report from a commander of the 5th to Major Juric, would that kind of document come up to you at the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer this specifically. As far as this document is concerned, it is addressed to Major Juric, who was the commander of the forward command post of the military police administration with the Split Military District at the time. Pursuant to my order on the establishment of the forward command posts, Major Juric was duty-bound to send reports to me every day by 2000 hours on the situation in his area of responsibility. Now, whether this is a document whereby he attempted to gather information or something else, I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we just look at paragraph 1. Because there it refers to members of the military police at Vrlika, forward command post were carrying out military police assignments -- regular military police assignments, sorry, by attending permanent barrier check-points, and doing car patrols. And those types of tasks, do they fall within the scope of regular as set out in Article 9 of the military police rules?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the tasks falling within the purview of the military police which are carried out regularly; or, second term, daily; or, third term, daily operational. In other words, tasks that are continuously carried out at a certain pace, in a certain area, following a certain method of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there anywhere within the military police rules or orders the definition of the word "regular," where a rule says, Regular means this, that, or the other?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer this question. However, in -- give me a moment to look at this. Yes, in the rules on the organisation and work of the military police, there is mention of the tasks performed by the military police. Perhaps I should clarify what extraordinary tasks means. On a given day, a certain military police unit, pursuant to the orders from their superior officer, has to carry out certain tasks by manning barrier check-points or some other assignments. At a certain moment on that particular day, there occurs an incident which, by its significance, calls for these forces of the military police to withdraw from performing the tasks that had been given to them, or were given to them in the daily work order, to abort their work at a particular check-point and to embark on that extraordinary task that was given to them as an order. Now, whether this amounts to an extraordinary expert of transportation or something else, it doesn't really matter. What matters is that both regular and extraordinary tasks should fall within the purview of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can now turn to another document. May that document, first of all, be admitted as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1295, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D47, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A document you have seen before, Mr. Lausic. It's dated the 14th of August, 1995. It's the one ending in 530. And it's your document issued to the battalions of the military police, and it concerns the implementation of the military and police tasks in the zones of responsibility of the military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 of the English, and I'm looking for paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's the last sentence in paragraph 11, if can you see that. I'll read it out. "In the daily operative command, the security commander of the 73rd Military Police Battalion is subordinated to the company commander of the military police in Knin and the commander of the 300th logistics base." And what I would like is, if you could explain the set-up that you had set down in this order in relation to the 73rd, the company commander of the military police, and the commander of the 300th logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best to give my comments, and you'll allow for the fact that a long time has elapsed since, to give my comments in relation to this particular item of the order. As we could see in the earlier orders, the 73rd Battalion, which was the battalion attached to the Croatian navy, was supposed to provide support to the 72nd Military Police Battalion. In this specific case, the military police took over the security of warehouses including the Golubic warehouse in Knin, and, pursuant to this order, the task would be carried out by the forces of the 73rd Military Police Battalion. Members of the 73rd Battalion, in the daily operational command -- or, rather, their commander is subordinated to the commander of the newly established military police company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion in Knin and to the commander of the 300th central logistics base of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia because it was securing their facility, the facility of the warehouse with his own men, the men of the military police units. The order is quite understandable and logical, the order resubordinating the commander of the security detail of the warehouse down the military police chain and down the chain of the commanders of the military -- of the Croatian army whose facility is being secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just looking, then, at the Knin company of the military police that was newly established, is it right that that company did not have its own number as part of the Split Military District? We have seen companies called the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th. But it was just called originally the joint company and then the independent company without having a designated number. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the term "independent company" was used. I don't think it was. The term used was the newly established company of the Military Police Knin or the Knin Military Police Company, but I can't be sure without consulting the documents. I don't think that "independent" was ever used because the company was established by the commander of the 72nd Battalion through his order, and that company was part of his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's right it did not have a number like the other companies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for it to be given a numerical designation, a process should come first whereby the 72nd Battalion's establishment book should be amended. This takes some time and is carried out on other levels of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the time that we're dealing with, that had not happened. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it also correct that it drew for its body of soldiers from the various other companies of the 72nd?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The commander of the 72nd Battalion drew upon the men that he had at his disposal in order to set up the company in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you aware that those men were not even paid as if from the Knin company, but they were still paid according to their units where they came from?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you aware that the units sent to the Knin company were allocated on a rotational basis? So for a period of two weeks, Commander Budimir would send some men from the 2nd, the 3rd, the 6th, and appoint them to be part of the Knin company for two weeks, as well as appointing the commander of the Knin company, again, on a period basis. Did you know that the system worked like that?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was fully within the competence of the commander of the 72nd Battalion, as was the case with all the other military police battalions from whose ranks the newly established military police units were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, turning to the next page, paragraph 14 of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before we do so, in paragraph 11, one line before the one you paid attention to, I think Mr. Misetic would again find the anti-tank where it's apparently is AT, anti-terrorist. You would agree that that is how we should read it? Yes, I leave it to you. It seems not to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: None of that is in dispute, and I had noticed that earlier in the day as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So looking at number 14 now, and this is it when the order is issued: "Normalize the command and control structure. Cover the entire zone of responsibility in daily reports through the duty service." And then sending separate reports. And then last sentence: "In the daily operational command, subordinate the commanders of the newly established platoons and companies of the Knin Military Police to the most senior Croatian army commander in the zone of responsibility and send the daily report to them." And I'm just going to ask you some questions now about that last sentence. We've looked at daily operational command. "The newly established platoons and companies of the Knin Military Police," that means the component parts of it, is that right? Traffic, regular military police, the duty service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, but I'm not sure I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at this sentence that begins, "In daily operational command ..." Have you got that? The last sentence in paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
